lessons.title: Technique reset
lessons.focus: Set up the guitar comfortably, identify the six strings and tune to standard pitch.
learningObjectives: Name the six strings from low to high (E–A–D–G–B–E) and describe the standard tuning targets.
Tune each string individually with a tuner, then recheck the full set after the first pass.
Demonstrate a supported seated or standing setup that lets both hands move without gripping or avoidable strain.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: A stable setup lets the hands focus on sound and movement instead of holding the instrument in place. Tuning is a comparison task: adjust one string toward its target, then recheck all six because changing string tension can slightly affect the others.
explanation.plainLanguage: Support the guitar with your body or strap, not with a tight fretting-hand grip. Tune one string at a time using small peg movements, then check the whole set again.
explanation.workedExample: Standard tuning check: from thickest to thinnest string, E2–A2–D3–G3–B3–E4. Use the tuner to verify each open string, then say the note names without looking.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a tuner display set to standard E–A–D–G–B–E and observe the learner's own comfortable instrument support. Do not treat one seated or standing posture as a universal body template.
steps: Support the guitar on your leg or with the strap so it stays in place without being held by the fretting hand.
Relax the shoulders and wrists; check that both hands can reach their normal playing areas without forcing the joint angle.
Name the strings from thickest to thinnest: low E, A, D, G, B, high E.
Set the tuner to standard tuning. Pluck one open string at a time and make small peg adjustments toward its target note.
Repeat the check from low E to high E after the first pass; retune any string that moved while the others were adjusted.
Play each open string once, listen for a stable pitch, and repeat the setup without reading the string list.

lessonBlocks.title: Hear the target
lessonBlocks.content: Listen to each open string separately. Notice whether the pitch is stable and whether the guitar remains supported when both hands are free to move.

lessonBlocks.title: Make music with it
lessonBlocks.content: Set up the instrument, tune and recheck all six strings, then play a slow low-to-high and high-to-low open-string check while naming each note.

lessonBlocks.title: Recall without looking
content: Which string needed the largest adjustment?
What supports the guitar so your fretting hand does not have to grip it?
What will you check first when you set up next time?

exercises.title: Listen, name and prepare
instructions: Place the guitar in your usual seated or standing position.
Check that the body or strap supports the instrument without a gripping hand.
Name all six strings from low to high before switching on the tuner.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner names E–A–D–G–B–E in order and can adjust the instrument support without creating discomfort.

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Tune low E, A, D, G, B and high E one at a time using small peg movements.
After the first pass, recheck each string in the same order and correct any drift.
Play each open string once and say its name before moving to the next.
exercises.successCriterion: The tuner indicates each string is within its in-tune range after a second check, and the learner identifies the six strings without relying on the display.

exercises.title: Musical application
instructions: Begin with the guitar already supported comfortably.
Play the six open strings low-to-high, then high-to-low, naming each pitch aloud.
Repeat once with the tuner hidden; reveal it afterward to verify the result.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner completes the setup and tuning sequence independently, names the strings in order and keeps the instrument supported while playing.

exercises.title: Recall and reflect
instructions: Put the string chart away and recall the six strings in order.
Record which string, if any, needed another tuning adjustment.
Choose one setup adjustment that makes the next practice session more comfortable.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner records a specific setup or tuning observation and can recall the string order without immediately viewing the reference.

musicalApplication.prompt: Set up and tune the guitar independently, then play and name each open string from low to high and back again.
instructions: Support the instrument before touching the tuning pegs.
Tune one string at a time and make a complete second pass.
Play each open string clearly and name the note without looking at the tuner display.
musicalApplication.sourcePolicy: Use original GuitarLab examples, learner-created material or properly licensed/public-domain repertoire; link to commercial song tabs rather than copying them.

successCriteria.criterion: Names all six standard-tuning strings from low to high: E–A–D–G–B–E.
Uses the tuner to bring each open string into its in-tune range and verifies the full set a second time.
The guitar remains supported while both hands are free to move; the learner does not rely on a tight fretting-hand grip.
Identifies and changes a setup position that creates avoidable tension or discomfort.
Repeats the setup and string-naming sequence without relying on a chart or step-by-step prompt.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Turning a tuning peg too far or continuing after the target pitch has been reached.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Make small adjustments, wait for the pitch reading to settle and recheck before turning again.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Holding the guitar in place by gripping the neck or raising the shoulder.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Adjust the body or strap support so the instrument stays stable without a gripping hand; pause and reset if discomfort appears.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Use a clip-on or screen-based tuner with a larger display, ask a helper to support the instrument during setup, or complete the string-naming task before tuning. Adapt seated/standing position to the learner's mobility and comfort.

lessons.title: Pentatonic across neck
lessons.focus: Connect two A minor pentatonic positions across the neck and compare their five notes with the C major scale.
learningObjectives: Play a short C major pattern and state its whole-step/half-step formula; identify how A minor pentatonic uses A–C–D–E–G.
Play A minor pentatonic box 1 and the adjacent box 2, naming the five notes and locating A as the tonal centre.
Create a short call-and-response phrase that moves between the two positions and resolves deliberately to A.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: The C major scale contains C–D–E–F–G–A–B. A minor pentatonic uses five notes from that same note collection—A, C, D, E and G—leaving out B and F. Two neighbouring fretboard positions let you keep the same musical idea while moving across the neck.
explanation.plainLanguage: Learn the five notes first, then find them in two nearby fretboard shapes. The shapes are maps of the same A minor pentatonic sound, not two different scales. Finish phrases on A so the tonal centre remains clear.
explanation.workedExample: A minor pentatonic box 1: low E 5–8, A 5–7, D 5–7, G 5–7, B 5–8, high e 5–8. Adjacent box 2: low E 8–10, A 7–10, D 7–10, G 7–9, B 8–10, high e 8–10.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a clear fretboard diagram showing A minor pentatonic box 1 at the fifth position and the adjacent box 2, with A-root notes highlighted. Demonstrate the shift slowly before adding a backing track.
steps: Play C major slowly and say the notes C–D–E–F–G–A–B; recall the formula whole–whole–half–whole–whole–whole–half.
Compare the note collection with A minor pentatonic: A–C–D–E–G. Say which two C-major notes are left out.
Play box 1 at the fifth position: low E 5–8, A 5–7, D 5–7, G 5–7, B 5–8, high e 5–8.
Play the adjacent box 2: low E 8–10, A 7–10, D 7–10, G 7–9, B 8–10, high e 8–10.
Connect the shapes slowly through the shared notes around the seventh-to-eighth-fret area; name A whenever you reach a root note.
Create a two-bar question and answer. Use notes from both positions and leave the final note on A.

lessonBlocks.title: Hear the target
lessonBlocks.content: Listen to a short A minor pentatonic phrase in two positions. Notice that the tone stays the same even as the hand moves to a new area of the neck.

lessonBlocks.title: Understand the idea
lessonBlocks.content: The C major scale contains C–D–E–F–G–A–B. A minor pentatonic uses five notes from that same note collection—A, C, D, E and G—leaving out B and F. Two neighbouring fretboard positions let you keep the same musical idea while moving across the neck.

lessonBlocks.content: Connect the two A minor pentatonic positions, then create a two-bar question-and-answer phrase. Use at least one note from each position and resolve the final note to A.

lessonBlocks.title: Recall without looking
content: Which five notes make up A minor pentatonic?
Where are the A-root notes in the two positions?
What changed when you moved the same phrase to the next box?

exercises.title: Listen, name and prepare
instructions: Say the C major notes and whole/half-step formula.
Name the five A minor pentatonic notes: A, C, D, E and G.
Find one A-root note in the fifth-position shape before playing the pattern.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner distinguishes the seven-note C major scale from the five-note A minor pentatonic set and identifies A as the tonic.

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Play A minor pentatonic box 1 ascending and descending at a slow, even pulse.
Play the adjacent box 2 and name the notes as they are reached.
Connect the positions through the shared fretboard area without restarting the pulse; pause and locate A again if the pattern becomes unclear.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner plays both positions with the correct A–C–D–E–G note set, identifies the root notes and connects the positions without losing the pulse.

exercises.title: Musical application
instructions: Choose a comfortable A minor backing or metronome pulse.
Play a two-bar question in box 1 and answer in box 2.
Leave a short space between phrases and resolve the final note to A.
exercises.successCriterion: The phrase uses both positions, keeps a clear pulse and resolves intentionally to A rather than ending on an arbitrary scale note.

exercises.title: Recall and reflect
instructions: Put the fretboard diagram away and name the five notes from memory.
Describe where the two positions connect and identify one A-root location.
Record which position needs another slow review.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner recalls the note set and records a specific position or transition to revisit.

musicalApplication.prompt: Create a two-bar A minor pentatonic call-and-response phrase using both adjacent positions and resolving to A.
instructions: Count in at a comfortable tempo.
Play the first phrase in box 1 and answer from box 2.
Leave space between the phrases and finish on an A-root note.

successCriteria.criterion: Plays the specified C major fragment and recalls the whole-step/half-step formula accurately.
Names and plays A–C–D–E–G without inserting B or F into the A minor pentatonic pattern.
Plays box 1 and box 2 with the stated string/fret locations and identifies A-root notes in each.
Moves between the two positions without losing the pattern or pulse.
Creates a short phrase using both positions and resolves it deliberately to A.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Treating the second box as a different scale or adding notes that are not in A minor pentatonic.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Say A–C–D–E–G before each run and check the note at each new position against that five-note set.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Playing the shapes mechanically without hearing A as the tonal centre.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Pause on an A-root note, sing it, then end the phrase on A and listen for the sense of resolution.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Practise the five-note set on one string first, use a slower tempo or smaller fretboard range, and connect only two strings before playing all six. A printed or enlarged fretboard map may remain available during early attempts.

lessons.title: Bends to pitch
lessons.focus: Bend a target pitch accurately and shape a short A minor pentatonic phrase over a blues pulse.
learningObjectives: Locate the G starting note and A target note on the B string, and compare the target with a fretted reference pitch.
Bend B-string fret 8 (G) up a whole step to match fret 10 (A), sustain it briefly and release with control.
Use one controlled bend in a short A minor pentatonic phrase, leaving musical space and maintaining the pulse.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: A bend raises a fretted note by increasing string tension. The target pitch should be heard and checked against a known reference note; the bend is not complete just because the string has moved. Support the bending finger, stop at the intended pitch and release without dropping the pulse.
explanation.plainLanguage: Play the note you want to reach first. Then fret the lower note and bend it until it sounds like that target. Keep the movement controlled, listen for the pitch and let the note return smoothly.
explanation.workedExample: On the B string, fret 10 and hear A. Fret 8 (G), bend it up one whole step until it matches the A reference, hold briefly and release to G. Use the bend once in a short A minor pentatonic phrase.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a close-up demonstration on the B string that first sounds the target A at fret 10, then bends G at fret 8 to match it. A tuner may support checking, but listening to the fretted reference is part of the task.
steps: On the B string, play fret 10 and listen carefully to the target A pitch.
Play fret 8 (G) on the same string, then bend it upward slowly until it matches the fretted A reference.
Use the index and middle fingers behind the bending finger for support; keep the wrist and thumb comfortable.
Hold the target briefly, release smoothly to G and compare the returned note with the original starting pitch.
Repeat at a slow pulse. If a whole-step bend is uncomfortable, use a smaller interval and compare it with the matching fretted target.
Place one controlled bend into a short A minor pentatonic phrase over an A blues pulse; leave space before the next idea.

lessonBlocks.title: Hear the target
lessonBlocks.content: Listen to the target note first, then hear the lower note bend toward it. Notice whether the bend arrives at the target pitch or stops short/overshoots.

lessonBlocks.title: Understand the idea
lessonBlocks.content: A bend raises a fretted note by increasing string tension. The target pitch should be heard and checked against a known reference note; the bend is not complete just because the string has moved. Support the bending finger, stop at the intended pitch and release without dropping the pulse.

lessonBlocks.title: Make music with it
lessonBlocks.content: Play a short A minor pentatonic phrase and include one whole-step bend from G to A on the B string. Keep the pulse, release the bend smoothly and leave space before the next phrase.

lessonBlocks.title: Recall without looking
content: What was the target pitch for the B-string fret 8 bend?

What changed when you placed the bend inside a phrase rather than practising it alone?

exercises.title: Listen, name and prepare
instructions: Play B-string fret 10 and sing or remember the target A.
Play B-string fret 8 and identify the starting G.
Check that the hand and wrist feel comfortable before attempting the bend.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner identifies G as the starting note and A as the target, and can hear the difference between them.

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Fret B-string fret 8 with a supported finger position.
Bend upward slowly until the pitch matches the fretted A at fret 10; use the target note as a reference between attempts.
Hold briefly, release to G and repeat at a slow pulse. Stop if the movement causes discomfort.
exercises.successCriterion: The bent note reaches the fretted A target without a clear undershoot/overshoot, sustains briefly and returns smoothly to G.

exercises.title: Musical application
instructions: Use an A minor backing or a steady pulse at a comfortable tempo.
Play a short phrase using A, C, D, E and G; include one G-to-A bend on the B string.
Leave space after the bend and resolve the phrase to A or another intended chord tone.
exercises.successCriterion: The bend reaches its intended pitch inside the phrase, the release is controlled and the learner keeps the musical pulse.

exercises.title: Recall and reflect
instructions: Listen back to the bend or repeat it once without the tuner display.
Record whether the target was reached and what helped the intonation.
Choose whether to repeat the same interval or reduce the bend range for the next session.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner records a specific pitch or comfort observation and chooses an appropriate next practice target.

musicalApplication.prompt: Play a short A minor pentatonic blues phrase with one controlled G-to-A bend on the B string.
instructions: Play the target A at B-string fret 10 before the phrase.
Use the G note at fret 8 and bend it to match the target.
Release smoothly, leave a beat of space and resolve the phrase deliberately.
musicalApplication.sourcePolicy: Use original GuitarLab examples, learner-created material or properly licensed/public-domain repertoire; link to commercial song tabs rather than copying them.

successCriteria.criterion: The B-string fret 8 bend reaches the A reference at fret 10 without a clear undershoot or overshoot.
The bent pitch is held briefly and released smoothly to the original G note.
The learner supports the bending finger and avoids forcing the wrist or grip.
The bend is integrated into a phrase using A minor pentatonic notes.
The phrase keeps a clear pulse, includes space and resolves intentionally after the bend.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Bending by feel without first hearing the target note.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Play the target fret first, then compare the bend to that known pitch on the same string.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Overshooting the target or forcing the hand to reach the interval.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Slow the movement, support the bending finger with the fingers behind it, or practise a smaller interval if needed.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Use a half-step bend to a fretted target on the same string, reduce the tempo, or sing the target before attempting the movement. Do not continue a bend that causes pain or strain.
retrievalPrompt: What note is the target for B-string fret 8 in this exercise?
How do you check whether the bend reaches the target pitch?
What helps you release the bend smoothly?

lessons.routeGoal: Develop more controlled lead playing, blues vocabulary, riffs and performance arrangements.
lessons.title: Legato control
lessons.focus: Coordinate alternate picking, clean two-string crossings and legato articulation with even timing and volume.
learningObjectives: Play a down-up picking sequence on one string and preserve the sequence when moving to a neighbouring string.
Cross from the D string to the G string with planned pick directions and without unintended string noise.
Perform a B-string hammer-on/pull-off cell without re-picking each note, keeping timing and volume even.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Core rhythm, clean fretting and basic chord/scale awareness as relevant to the selected specialisation.

explanation.keyIdea: Alternate picking uses a planned down-up sequence. String crossing means carrying that sequence to the next string without resetting automatically. Legato uses fretting-hand movement—such as hammer-ons and pull-offs—to sound connected notes without picking every pitch. These are related but distinct skills and need separate checks.
explanation.plainLanguage: Practise the picking pattern and the legato pattern separately first. Keep the pick moving down-up as you cross strings. For legato, pick the first note, hammer to the higher fret, pull back and hammer again without extra pick strokes.
explanation.workedExample: Picking: D string 5–7 then G string 5–7 with down-up-down-up. Legato: B string 5–7–5–7—pick fret 5, hammer to 7, pull to 5, then hammer to 7.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Show a close-up picking-hand view for the D-to-G string crossing and a fretting-hand view for the B-string 5–7–5–7 legato cell. Demonstrate each movement separately before combining them.
steps: Hold the pick without a rigid grip and expose only enough tip to contact the string.
On the D string, play frets 5 and 7 using down then up strokes.
Continue to the G string at frets 5 and 7, preserving the next down-up strokes rather than restarting the pattern.
Play the picking cell slowly and listen for even timing and attack across the string change.
On the B string, pick fret 5, hammer to fret 7, pull back to fret 5 and hammer to fret 7; do not pick each legato note.
Compare the timing and volume of the four legato notes, then join the picking and legato cells in a short phrase.

lessonBlocks.title: Hear the target
lessonBlocks.content: Listen for an even down-up attack across two strings, then compare it with a connected legato phrase in which the fretting hand sounds several notes after one pick attack.

lessonBlocks.title: Understand the idea
lessonBlocks.content: Alternate picking uses a planned down-up sequence. String crossing means carrying that sequence to the next string without resetting automatically. Legato uses fretting-hand movement—such as hammer-ons and pull-offs—to sound connected notes without picking every pitch. These are related but distinct skills and need separate checks.

lessonBlocks.title: See and try it slowly
content: Hold the pick without a rigid grip and expose only enough tip to contact the string.
On the D string, play frets 5 and 7 using down then up strokes.
Continue to the G string at frets 5 and 7, preserving the next down-up strokes rather than restarting the pattern.
Play the picking cell slowly and listen for even timing and attack across the string change.
On the B string, pick fret 5, hammer to fret 7, pull back to fret 5 and hammer to fret 7; do not pick each legato note.
Compare the timing and volume of the four legato notes, then join the picking and legato cells in a short phrase.

lessonBlocks.title: Make music with it

content: Where did the pick sequence change or reset during the string crossing?

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Play D-string frets 5–7 then G-string frets 5–7 using down-up-down-up strokes.

Play B-string frets 5–7–5–7: pick the first note, hammer to 7, pull to 5 and hammer to 7. Keep the three unpicked notes clear and even.
exercises.successCriterion: The D-to-G crossing preserves the D–U–D–U sequence, and the legato cell sounds four distinct notes without re-picking the hammer-on/pull-off notes.

successCriteria.criterion: The pick follows the intended down-up sequence on the four-note picking cell.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Restarting every string with a downstroke even when the alternate-picking sequence calls for an upstroke.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Say D–U–D–U aloud and practise the two-string cell slowly before adding more notes.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Pulling off too weakly or lifting the finger so far that the next note loses timing.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Use a small controlled fretting-hand movement and compare the volume of picked and unpicked notes.

lessons.title: Blues shuffle arrangement
lessons.focus: Play a 12-bar A blues shuffle with the quick-change D7 bar, a steady long-short swing feel and a clear E7 turnaround.
learningObjectives: Count a steady beat and explain the shuffle as a long-short eighth-note feel drawn from a triplet subdivision.
Play a two-note root-and-fifth shuffle figure for A7, D7 and E7 while changing position without losing the pulse.
Perform the 12-bar quick-change form in A, including the E7 turnaround that leads back to A7.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: A shuffle keeps the quarter-note pulse steady while dividing each beat into a long-short pair, commonly felt as the first and third parts of a triplet. The harmony supplies the form: A7 is the I chord, D7 the IV chord and E7 the V chord. In this quick-change version, bar 2 moves to D7; bar 12 uses E7 as a turnaround into the next chorus.
explanation.plainLanguage: Keep counting four even beats in each bar. Make the two shuffle notes feel uneven but repeatable: a longer first note and a shorter second note. Move the same root-fifth idea with the chord, and do not let the change disturb the beat.
explanation.workedExample: Quick-change 12-bar in A: | A7 | D7 | A7 | A7 | D7 | D7 | A7 | A7 | E7 | D7 | A7 | E7 |. A simple two-note figure is A–E (low E string fret 5 and A string fret 7), D–A (A string fret 5 and D string fret 7), then E–B (A string fret 7 and D string fret 9).

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use an original GuitarLab demonstration or a teacher-created backing/example. Keep commercial recordings as listening references only; do not reproduce protected tabs, riffs or lesson text. A metronome, tuner or learner recording may be used where helpful.
steps: Tap four even quarter-note beats and count each beat as a triplet: 1-trip-let, 2-trip-let, 3-trip-let, 4-trip-let.
Play only the first and third triplet positions as a long-short pair. Keep the count moving evenly; do not speed up to make the shuffle feel stronger.
On A7, alternate A at low E fret 5 with E at A fret 7. Use a light, repeatable attack and mute the strings between notes.
Move the same root-fifth idea to D7: D at A fret 5 and A at D fret 7. Then move to E7: E at A fret 7 and B at D fret 9.
Play the 12 bars in order: A7, D7, A7, A7, D7, D7, A7, A7, E7, D7, A7, E7. Say each chord name at the start of its bar.
Loop bars 9–12 slowly. Let E7 create the turnaround and return to A7 on the next bar 1 without adding an extra beat.

lessonBlocks.title: Hear the musical target
lessonBlocks.content: Listen to a straight pair of eighth notes, then to a shuffled long-short pair over the same steady beat. Notice that the subdivision changes but the quarter-note pulse does not. Follow the bass/root movement as the progression moves from A7 to D7 and E7.

lessonBlocks.content: Perform two choruses of the quick-change A blues: keep the shuffle figure consistent in the first, then add one simple muted or accented variation in the second without changing the form.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Making the shuffle pair so uneven that the quarter-note beat becomes unstable.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Tap the quarter notes separately, count triplets aloud and place the two played notes on the first and third triplet positions.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Changing to D7 or E7 one beat late because the left hand is not ready.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Loop only the two bars around the change, prepare the next root before bar 1 of the new chord and keep counting through the move.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Letting open or adjacent strings ring between the two-note attacks.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Release pressure just enough to stop the previous note and use the picking-hand edge or unused fingers for light muting.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Begin by tapping or speaking the shuffle while a helper or backing loop plays the chord changes. lessons.title: Quarter review: lead tone
lessons.focus: Review the first five Rock & Blues lessons by recording one A blues lead chorus and evaluating pulse, note clarity, bend intonation, legato and phrase shape.
learningObjectives: Prepare and record one uninterrupted 12-bar A blues lead take with a count-in and a steady pulse.
Include a connected A minor pentatonic phrase, one controlled B-string G-to-A bend and one clear legato figure without crowding every bar.
Review the recording for one specific tone or phrasing strength and choose one observable next improvement.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: A useful review take is a snapshot of musical choices, not a pass/fail test. Lead tone comes from controllable elements such as attack, note length, muting, dynamics and intonation as well as equipment settings. Keep the sound setup consistent while reviewing, so you can hear what your hands and phrasing change.
explanation.plainLanguage: Record a complete chorus without stopping after a small mistake. Listen for whether notes speak clearly, bends reach their target, legato notes stay even and phrases leave space. Choose one change for the next take rather than trying to fix everything at once.
explanation.workedExample: Plan a 12-bar lead chorus over the A7/D7/E7 shuffle: use box 1 for the opening phrase, connect into box 2, place a B-string fret 8 G-to-fret 10 A bend in a later phrase, and use the B-string 5–7–5–7 legato cell once. Leave at least one phrase ending with space before the next idea.

steps: Tune the guitar and choose a comfortable sound level. Keep amp, instrument and recording settings unchanged between review takes.
Use an original A blues backing loop, a metronome with a simple A pulse, or a teacher-recorded accompaniment. Confirm the 12-bar form before starting.
Count in and record one full chorus. Play a short A minor pentatonic phrase, connect box 1 to box 2, include one B-string fret 8 G-to-fret 10 A bend and use one B-string 5–7–5–7 legato cell.
Leave rests between phrases. Keep the pulse through a rest and continue to the next safe bar if a note is missed.
Listen back once for pulse and form, once for bend intonation and note clarity, and once for phrase shape and muting.
Choose one target for a second take, such as a more accurate bend, cleaner release, quieter unwanted strings or a clearer phrase ending.

lessons.title: Chord-tone soloing
lessons.focus: Target the major third and flat seventh of A7, D7 and E7 so lead phrases follow the changing harmony in a 12-bar blues.
learningObjectives: Name the four chord tones in A7 (A–C#–E–G), D7 (D–F#–A–C) and E7 (E–G#–B–D).
Land on the major third or flat seventh of the current chord at a chord change, then connect to the next target with a nearby note.
Build a short A blues solo that combines chord tones with A minor pentatonic passing notes and resolves deliberately.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: A dominant seventh chord contains a root, major third, fifth and flat seventh. In an A blues, the harmony changes from A7 to D7 and E7, so a note that sounds settled over one chord may sound different over the next. Targeting the third or flat seventh makes the chord change audible; pentatonic notes can connect those targets rather than replacing them.
explanation.plainLanguage: Do not run the same scale shape without listening to the chords. Name the chord, choose one of its important notes and aim for it when the chord changes. Begin with the thirds: C# over A7, F# over D7 and G# over E7.
explanation.workedExample: Chord tones: A7 = A, C#, E, G; D7 = D, F#, A, C; E7 = E, G#, B, D. First pass: play C# when A7 is heard, F# when D7 arrives and G# when E7 arrives. Second pass: add the flat sevenths G, C and D as alternate targets.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use an original GuitarLab demonstration or a teacher-created backing/example. Keep commercial recordings as listening references only; do not reproduce protected tabs, riffs or lesson text. A metronome, tuner or learner recording may be used where helpful.
steps: Say the chord tones for A7, D7 and E7 aloud before playing: A–C#–E–G; D–F#–A–C; E–G#–B–D.
Find one comfortable location for C# and play it over A7; listen for how it sits against the chord.
When the progression moves to D7, change the target to F#. When it moves to E7, target G#. Keep the target on a clear beat rather than rushing to fill the bar.
Repeat using the flat seventh targets G over A7, C over D7 and D over E7.
Add one or two A minor pentatonic notes between targets. If using C natural over A7 as a blues inflection, treat it as a colour that resolves to C# or another stable chord tone.
Play the quick-change 12-bar form and aim for the correct chord tone at each I, IV or V change.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Playing A minor pentatonic continuously without noticing when D7 or E7 arrives.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Pause on the chord change, name the chord and land first on its third or flat seventh before adding connecting notes.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Treating C natural and C# as interchangeable stable notes over A7.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Hear C natural as a blues inflection; resolve or bend it toward C# when the phrase needs the A7 major-third colour.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Trying to play all four chord tones quickly before the target notes are secure.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Use one target note per chord change first. Add a second chord tone only after the first target is clear by ear and on the fretboard.

lessons.title: Riff construction
lessons.focus: Compose a memorable one- or two-bar rock-blues riff from A minor pentatonic notes, a repeatable rhythm and deliberate rests or mutes.
learningObjectives: Choose a compact three-to-five-note motif from A minor pentatonic and play it cleanly in one fretboard position.
Repeat the motif with a steady pulse, then vary one feature such as the final note, accent, rhythm or register.
Create and record an original riff that fits an A7 shuffle and uses rests or muting to make its rhythm distinct.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: A riff is a short musical idea whose identity comes from its rhythm, pitch shape and repetition. It becomes memorable when the listener can recognise the motif, then hear a deliberate variation. A rest is part of the riff: mute the strings and keep the pulse moving instead of filling every gap.
explanation.plainLanguage: Start with a small note group and a clear rhythm. Repeat it so it becomes recognisable. Change only one thing on the next pass, and use a rest or muted beat to make the groove feel intentional.
explanation.workedExample: A one-bar idea from A minor pentatonic box 1: low E fret 5 (A), rest, low E fret 8 (C), A-string fret 5 (D), A-string fret 7 (E), rest, A-string fret 5 (D), low E fret 5 (A). Keep the same rhythm on the repeat, then change only the final A to C for a variation.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use an original GuitarLab demonstration or a teacher-created backing/example. Keep commercial recordings as listening references only; do not reproduce protected tabs, riffs or lesson text. A metronome, tuner or learner recording may be used where helpful.
steps: Use A minor pentatonic box 1: low E 5–8, A 5–7, D 5–7, G 5–7, B 5–8 and high e 5–8. Choose only three to five notes for the first motif.
Play the example motif slowly: A (low E 5), rest, C (low E 8), D (A 5), E (A 7), rest, D (A 5), A (low E 5).
Count the rests and lightly mute the strings during them; do not let open strings ring into the next note.
Repeat the same motif twice with the same rhythm and attack so its identity is clear.
Create a second version by changing only one feature: the final note, one accent, the register or the timing of one attack.
Play the riff over an A7 shuffle and check that the rhythmic pattern fits the groove without rushing the bar line.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Adding new notes every time the riff repeats until its identity disappears.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Keep the original rhythm and note shape for two repetitions; make only one planned change on the variation.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Filling every rest with another note or allowing strings to ring.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Count the empty beat and mute the strings deliberately so silence is part of the riff.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Choosing notes that are comfortable under the fingers but do not fit the intended A minor pentatonic idea.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Name each chosen note and check it against A, C, D, E or G before adding it to the motif.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Begin with a two- or three-note motif on one string, tap the rhythm before playing and use a slower pulse. A learner with limited fretting reach may use open-position notes from the same A minor pentatonic collection or record a hummed rhythm before choosing notes.

lessons.title: Modal colour
lessons.focus: Hear and use A Mixolydian over A7 by contrasting its G natural flat seventh with the G# in A major, then resolve phrases to A7 chord tones.
learningObjectives: Name and play the A Mixolydian notes A–B–C#–D–E–F#–G and state its 1–2–3–4–5–6–b7 formula.
Compare A Mixolydian with A major and hear G natural as the flat-seventh colour over A7.
Create a short phrase over an A7 vamp that uses G purposefully and resolves to A, C# or E.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: Mixolydian is a major-scale mode with a lowered seventh degree. A Mixolydian contains A–B–C#–D–E–F#–G; A major has G#. A7 contains A–C#–E–G, so the G natural reinforces the dominant-seventh sound. This colour is useful over A7, but it should not be applied blindly to every chord in an A blues: D7 and E7 have their own chord tones and can be approached with the targets from Week 7 or their own Mixolydian centres.
explanation.plainLanguage: Play A major, then lower G# to G natural. Listen to how the sound becomes more blues-rock and dominant. Use G as a colour note, then land on a note from A7—A, C# or E—to make the phrase feel settled.
explanation.workedExample: A Mixolydian: A–B–C#–D–E–F#–G. A7 chord tones: A–C#–E–G. Play the scale slowly over an A7 vamp, pause on G, then resolve to A or C#. Compare the G natural with G# from A major. Over D7 or E7, use the chord tones from Week 7 or shift the modal centre rather than treating A Mixolydian as a universal scale.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use an original GuitarLab demonstration or a teacher-created backing/example. Keep commercial recordings as listening references only; do not reproduce protected tabs, riffs or lesson text. A metronome, tuner or learner recording may be used where helpful.
steps: Play or sing A major: A–B–C#–D–E–F#–G#. Identify the seventh degree G#.
Lower only that note to G natural to form A Mixolydian: A–B–C#–D–E–F#–G.
Play A7 (A–C#–E–G) or use an A7 backing vamp, then play the A Mixolydian notes slowly in one position.
Pause on G natural and listen to its dominant-seventh colour. Resolve the phrase to A, C# or E rather than stopping on an uncertain note.
Create a two-bar phrase that uses G once and C# or A as a clear landing tone. Repeat it with a different rhythm.

When the backing changes to D7 or E7, stop using A Mixolydian as an automatic blanket scale. Target the chord tones from Week 7, or explore D Mixolydian over D7 and E Mixolydian over E7 as a separate extension.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Playing A major with G# and calling it A Mixolydian.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Check the seventh degree: A Mixolydian uses G natural, while A major uses G#.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Playing A Mixolydian unchanged over the entire A7–D7–E7 progression.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Keep the comparison over A7 first. When the chord changes, target its chord tones or deliberately shift to the corresponding D or E Mixolydian centre.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Ending every phrase on G because it is the new colour note.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Let G create the dominant tension, then resolve to A, C# or E when the phrase needs a stable landing.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Use an A7 drone or a two-chord A7 vamp and compare only G# with G natural before playing the full mode. The learner may sing the two notes, play a one-octave fragment or use a printed note list. A major pentatonic comparison can replace the full scale during the first pass.
retrievalPrompt: What is the seventh note in A Mixolydian, and how does it differ from A major?
Which A7 chord tones can resolve the G natural?
Why should A Mixolydian not automatically be used over D7 and E7?

lessons.title: Phrasing and silence
lessons.focus: Shape short blues phrases with call-and-response, deliberate rests and clear rhythmic placement while keeping the pulse moving.
learningObjectives: Play a one-bar A minor pentatonic question phrase and leave a measured rest before the response.
Answer the question with a related motif that changes one rhythmic or melodic feature.
Maintain the underlying pulse through silence and resolve the response to a chord tone or intended A-centred note.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: Phrasing gives a melody a beginning, direction and ending. Call-and-response makes that shape audible: one phrase asks a question and a second phrase answers it. Silence is active musical space, not a loss of time; count through the rest so the response enters deliberately.
explanation.plainLanguage: Play a short idea, stop the strings and keep counting, then answer it. Reuse part of the first idea so the two phrases sound related. Change the rhythm or ending, not everything at once.
explanation.workedExample: Over an A blues pulse, play a short question using A–C–D, leave beat 4 silent, then answer with E–D–C–A. Keep the quarter-note count moving through the rest and land the answer on A or another appropriate chord tone.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use an original GuitarLab demonstration or a teacher-created backing/example. steps: Choose three or four A minor pentatonic notes in one position and make a one-bar question phrase.
Play the question once, then mute the strings and count the next beat or bar aloud without filling the space.
Create an answer from the same motif. Change one feature such as the final note, rhythm, register or direction.
Resolve the answer to A or to a chord tone that fits the current harmony. Sing the final note before playing it.
Repeat the question-and-answer pair over a steady pulse. Keep the rests the same length each time.
Record the pair and listen for phrase shape, timing, silence and whether the answer sounds connected to the question.

successCriteria.criterion: Creates a short question phrase with a clear beginning and an intentional response rather than an unstructured note run.
Counts through rests, keeps the pulse and mutes strings so silence is audible and intentional.
The response reuses a recognisable part of the question while changing one deliberate feature.
Ends the response on A or another note that fits the current chord and can explain the choice.
Uses note length, dynamics or articulation to make the two phrases sound distinct without rushing.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Filling every rest with extra notes because silence feels like stopping.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Count the empty beat aloud and mute the strings. The pulse continues even when the guitar is silent.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Making the answer completely unrelated to the question.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Reuse the opening rhythm or two-note shape and change just one feature so the listener can hear the connection.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Ending on a note without listening to the backing chord.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Sing the intended landing note, check the current chord and resolve to A or one of its chord tones where appropriate.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Use a two-note motif and a longer rest before adding more notes. The learner may speak or clap the question-and-answer rhythm, use a metronome with a slower beat, or work over a single A7 drone before adding the full blues changes.

nextReviewSuggestion.adaptation: If the learner loses the pulse during silence, shorten the phrase and lengthen the countable rest. Add variation only after the question and answer remain in time.

lessons.title: Performance arrangement
lessons.focus: Arrange an A blues performance with an intro, 12-bar head, contrasting lead chorus, return and intentional ending.
learningObjectives: Map a short arrangement as a two-bar intro, 12-bar theme/head, 12-bar lead chorus and a short ending tag.
Practise the transitions between sections and choose a dynamic or texture change that makes the arrangement easy to follow.
Perform the arrangement from count-in to ending and recover at a planned bar if a note or transition is missed.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.

explanation.keyIdea: An arrangement gives the listener a route through the music. The same 12-bar harmony can support an intro, a recognisable riff or head, a contrasting solo and a return or ending. Clear section cues, deliberate dynamics and rehearsed transitions make a performance feel complete even when individual notes are not perfect.
explanation.plainLanguage: Decide what happens first, what changes in the middle and how the piece ends. Keep the same blues form underneath, but change the role of the guitar between the riff section and the solo section. Practise the joins before running the whole arrangement.
explanation.workedExample: A compact A blues arrangement: 2-bar intro on the riff; 12-bar head with the main riff; 12-bar solo chorus using pentatonic phrases and chord-tone targets; 2-bar ending tag that resolves to A. Count in before the intro and agree on the last hit or sustained A ending.

steps: Choose the original riff from Week 8 or create a simple two-bar head that fits the 12-bar A blues.
Write a section map: count-in, two-bar intro, 12-bar head, 12-bar solo chorus and two-bar ending tag.
Decide how the solo section differs from the head—use a lighter texture, more space, a gradual dynamic build or a different register.
Mark the bar where the head returns or the ending tag begins. Practise the last two bars of each section into the first two bars of the next.
Choose one recovery point, such as the start of the next 4-bar phrase, so a missed note does not stop the pulse.
Record one full arrangement without stopping, then listen for section clarity, transitions, dynamics and the final ending.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: The solo section starts without a clear cue, so the form becomes hard to follow.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Mark the transition bar and use a count, fill or dynamic change that signals the new section.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: The head and solo sound identical because only more notes are added.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Choose one purposeful contrast such as a sparser head, higher solo register or a gradual dynamic arc.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Stopping the whole arrangement after a missed note.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Keep counting and rejoin at the agreed recovery point; review the missed transition after the complete take.

lessons.title: Path capstone
lessons.focus: Present an original Rock & Blues capstone that combines a 12-bar A blues form, shuffle or groove, riff, lead chorus, chord-tone targets, expressive phrasing and a planned ending.
learningObjectives: Prepare an original blues arrangement with a clear form, count-in, recognisable head or riff and an intentional ending.
Perform a lead section that combines A minor pentatonic vocabulary, at least one controlled expressive technique and chord-aware phrase resolution.
Record or perform a complete take, recover through small slips and reflect on evidence for one strength and one next improvement.
priorTopicsToRefresh: Use a comfortable guitar setup and standard tuning.
Retrieve A minor pentatonic notes A–C–D–E–G, the neighbouring box connection, target-pitch bends and controlled legato from the previous Rock & Blues lessons.

explanation.keyIdea: The capstone is a transfer task: combine the route's techniques and vocabulary in music rather than repeating isolated drills. A strong performance shows a clear form and pulse, purposeful use of the riff, phrases that respond to the harmony, controlled articulation and an ending the listener can recognise. A short, complete performance is more useful than a long arrangement that loses its shape.
explanation.plainLanguage: Make a short original blues performance that shows what you can now do. Keep the groove and form clear, use the riff as an identity, make the solo sound connected to the chords, and finish deliberately. Record it, listen back and choose one next step.
explanation.workedExample: Full version: count-in; two-bar intro; 12-bar A blues head; 12-bar lead chorus with a box 1-to-box 2 connection, a G-to-A bend, a legato figure, chord-tone landings over A7/D7/E7 and phrase space; two-bar ending tag. Short version: one 12-bar chorus with the riff, one contrasting lead phrase and a planned ending.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use an original GuitarLab demonstration or a teacher-created backing/example. Keep commercial recordings as listening references only; do not reproduce protected tabs, riffs or lesson text. A metronome, tuner or learner recording may be used where helpful.
steps: Choose or compose an original two-bar riff/head in A and confirm that it sits over the quick-change 12-bar form.
Choose the performance length: full version with head and solo choruses, or the accessible one-chorus version with a clear riff and contrasting lead phrase.
Map the count-in, section order, chord changes and ending tag. Mark at least one planned recovery point.
Plan the lead chorus: connect pentatonic positions, include one controlled bend or legato gesture, target the current chord's third or flat seventh and leave space between phrases.
Rehearse the hardest transition and the ending tag separately, then perform one complete take without stopping for small mistakes.

lessonBlocks.title: Understand the musical idea
lessonBlocks.content: The capstone is a transfer task: combine the route's techniques and vocabulary in music rather than repeating isolated drills. A strong performance shows a clear form and pulse, purposeful use of the riff, phrases that respond to the harmony, controlled articulation and an ending the listener can recognise. A short, complete performance is more useful than a long arrangement that loses its shape.

Listen back or invite a trusted listener to review form, pulse, note clarity, harmonic phrasing and ending. Choose one priority for a later retake.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Trying to demonstrate every technique in every bar, which makes the performance crowded.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Choose one or two moments for the bend and legato, then let the riff, rests and chord changes shape the rest of the solo.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Losing the 12-bar form while concentrating on the lead technique.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Rehearse the form with chord names or a backing loop first and use a clear recovery point if a phrase goes wrong.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Treating recording quality, speed or number of notes as the main measure of success.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Review the musical criteria separately: form, groove, note clarity, harmony, phrasing and ending. Choose one next target rather than assigning a single pass score.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: The capstone can be a complete one-chorus performance rather than two choruses. explanation.keyIdea: Fingerstyle assigns musical roles to the picking hand. The thumb commonly handles bass strings while index, middle and ring fingers play treble strings. Independence develops by stabilising each part before combining them.
explanation.plainLanguage: This lesson focuses on right-hand independence — build independent fingerstyle, bass movement, chord melody and acoustic arrangement skills.. First understand the sound or movement, then practise a small part, then return to the musical whole. Treat the written checkpoint as an observable target, not a deadline.
explanation.workedExample: Create or perform an original 4- to 8-bar example demonstrating right-hand independence.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use a clear, slow demonstration of right-hand independence — build independent fingerstyle, bass movement, chord melody and acoustic arrangement skills. from a reputable guitar-learning source or your own view of the fretboard. steps: Rest the picking hand comfortably and assign the thumb to the bass strings and fingers to the treble strings.

lessonBlocks.title: Understand the idea
lessonBlocks.content: A chord is a group of notes heard together. Its name describes the root and quality; a guitar shape is one way to arrange those notes. Check the intended strings individually before adding rhythm, and listen for how the chord functions in the progression.

lessonBlocks.title: See and try it slowly
content: Set up the instrument comfortably and check that the exercise is pain-free.
Name the chord and identify its root; use the stated chord map or a diagram as a starting point.
Place fingers close to the fret wires and keep excluded strings muted or untouched.
Pick each intended string separately, correct any buzzing or muted note, then strum a slow pulse.
Work on this week's target: Create or perform an original 4- to 8-bar example demonstrating reharmonisation.. Begin below the suggested reference tempo if accuracy is not yet secure.
Apply the skill in a musical phrase or progression; keep the pulse going through a small error.
Finish by recalling the key idea without looking and recording one observation.

lessonBlocks.title: Make music with it
lessonBlocks.content: Apply the skill to Create or perform an original 4- to 8-bar example demonstrating reharmonisation.. Preserve the pulse and give the phrase a clear beginning and ending.

lessonBlocks.title: Recall without looking
content: What is the root of the chord you practised?
What changed in the sound when the chord quality or voicing changed?

exercises.title: Listen, name and prepare
instructions: Say what you are trying to make sound or demonstrate.
Listen to a reference or hum the target before playing.
Choose a comfortable starting tempo and one observable quality target.
exercises.successCriterion: You can state the target and identify what a successful attempt should sound or feel like.

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Form each chord or voicing in the lesson. Arpeggiate the intended strings, correct one issue at a time, then change to the next shape without squeezing.
Work in short sets; pause to identify and correct one specific issue before repeating.
Only increase tempo after clean, relaxed repetitions; reduce it if accuracy or comfort declines.
exercises.successCriterion: Every intended chord tone is clear, excluded strings are controlled, and the learner can identify the chord name, root or quality.

instructions: Apply the week's exercise: Create or perform an original 4- to 8-bar example demonstrating reharmonisation..
